newsitem.title: UK: Oil price, Mideast market share seen flat to 2010.
newsitem.headline: Oil price, Mideast market share seen flat to 2010.

text.p: Oil prices are unlikely to rise sharply between now and the year 2010 with Middle Eastern oil producers (OPEC and non-OPEC) unlikely to see their market share rise much above current levels of just over 30 percent, a book just published by a leading think tank concludes.

"The idea that we are sitting on an escalator that will carry us to higher prices because of Middle East dominance does not seem likely," the principle author, John Mitchell, said at the launch of his book, "The New Geopolitics of Energy."
Mitchell is chairman of the Energy and Environmental Programme at the Royal Institute for International Affairs (RIIA).

The book says production from non-OPEC countries or what Mitchell calls the "oil machine" is likely to maintain a growth rate of 600,000 barrels per day (bpd) to the year 2010, at the expense of OPEC producers.

"Oil production outside OPEC, and outside the Middle East, is likely to continue to rise until 2010 so that the share of OPEC and Middle Eastern supplies in the world oil market may not increase," it adds.
"In this projection, the Middle East share of world oil production remains close to 30 percent through the next ten years, rising to 31 percent by 2010."

The book says that if the highest demand projection of 95 million bpd is taken and the difference met entirely from the Middle East -- which includes non-OPEC Arab producers -- this share would rise to the 1975 level of 36 percent.

"The analysis above suggests that the dynamics of oil production and demand, at least until 2010, do not support the idea that the call on OPEC will grow rapidly to unprecedented levels which would make cartelization simple..."

Mitchell said the political, economic and rivalries between the disparate producers in the Middle East meant they were unlikely to adopt a cohesive policy to engineer a sustained rise in prices even when their share of the market began to grow again after 2010.

Although these rivalries increased the risk of supply disruptions from the Middle East -- which the book estimates contains 54 percent of the world's remaining identified reserves -- this would not necessarily lead to a sustained rise in prices.

"The timing of oil developments is not hurried by market prospects...Demand for Middle East oil may not increase significantly beyond 2000 and by 2010 may increase by only 7.0 million bpd," the book says.

"Oil prices are unlikely to show a long-term trend before 2010 but may rise or fall during investment cycles and short-term market disruptions. The prospect of a long-term aggressive oil price cartel is remote," a summary of the book says.
